title: Shark Tank Style Pitch
goal: Your kid asks the family for real backing, Shark Tank style. They build the numbers for their business, decide exactly what they're asking for and what the shark gets back, write a one-minute pitch, face a panel of family sharks, then sign a real deal and keep it.
need: A business idea, new or already running
A little real money to invest, or another kind of help
Family members to be the sharks
Paper for the pitch and the deal

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: You're a shark, and a fair one. Your most useful question is 'What does the shark get?' Use real money and keep it small, because a $20 loan they actually pay back teaches more than a pretend million. Anyone in the family can be a shark, siblings included.

plan.what: Build the numbers and choose the deal (Steps 1 and 2).

troubleshoot.q: They don't have a business yet
troubleshoot.a: Borrow one from Micro-Business Challenge or Complaint to Product, or keep it tiny. A batch of cookies to sell counts.
Start with one shark, sitting down. Nerves usually drop once they hear the first question.

troubleshoot.q: They can't pay it back on time
troubleshoot.a: That's a real lesson, if it's handled well. Help them ask the shark for new terms before the date, then keep the new promise.

lesson.text: A good ask isn't a favour. It says exactly what the money is for, what the shark gets back and how it gets paid.
lesson.before: Can I have $30 for my business? Please?

model.line: I'll pay you back $22 by March 1, from bracelet sales.
I keep $1.50 from each bracelet, so 15 bracelets pays you back.

lesson.modelNote: The first ask was a favour. The second tells the shark what it's for, what they get and how it gets paid, so they can say yes for a reason.

steps.title: Build your numbers
steps.why: Sharks invest in numbers, not just ideas.
steps.kid: Your kid brings the numbers from a business they've run, or works out new ones, with the Numbers card in the Shark Toolkit at the end of the guide: what they need to start, what they have, the gap and how many sales it takes to pay back.
steps.you: Check the costs against real prices, in a shop or online. Let them do the math, and ask 'How do you know?' about every number.
ask: What do you need to get started?
How much is left from each sale?
steps.tip: Count what they already have first. Asking for $20 sounds very different when they've saved $10 themselves.

levels.explore: Say what you'd sell, the price and what you need to buy first.
levels.develop: Work out the cost of one, what's left from each sale and the total you need.
levels.extend: Work out how many you'd need to sell to pay back the start-up money.

steps.title: Choose your deal
steps.why: The ask isn't 'Can I have money?' It's what the shark gets back.
steps.kid: Your kid decides what they're asking for and what they'll offer in return, using the Deal options card: a loan they pay back with a little extra, a share of the profits for a set time, or help instead of money. They work out exactly what the shark gets.
steps.you: Explain how a loan and a share are different, with an example from your own life if you have one. Keep the amounts small and real.
steps.tip: A deal needs a date. 'I'll pay you back' becomes a real offer the moment it has one.

levels.explore: Ask for something small, and say how you'll pay it back.
levels.develop: Write a loan offer with an amount, a date and a little extra.
levels.extend: Compare a loan and a share, work out what the shark gets from each and choose one.

steps.title: Write the one-minute pitch
steps.why: Sharks decide fast, so every second needs a job.
steps.kid: Your kid writes a pitch using the Pitch parts card: the hook, the problem, the solution, the numbers and the ask. They time it at a minute or less, then practise until they can say it without reading.
steps.you: Be the practice audience twice. The first time, just listen. The second time, tell them the one part you didn't understand.
ask: Could a shark repeat your ask after hearing it once?
steps.tip: End with the ask, in one sentence with numbers in it. It's the line the sharks will remember.

levels.explore: Say each part of the pitch out loud, with a grown-up helping.
levels.develop: Write and time a one-minute pitch, then practise it three times.
levels.extend: Add a sample or one picture, and practise answering the two questions you're most worried about.

steps.title: Face the sharks
steps.why: The questions are where a pitch is really won.
steps.kid: Your kid pitches to a panel of family sharks, who ask questions and score it using the Shark panel card. Each shark makes an offer, changes the terms or says 'I'm out'. Your kid decides: accept, ask for something different or walk away.
steps.you: Be a real shark: kind, but not easy. Only offer what you'd honestly put in. Let a sibling take a turn as a shark too. Keep sibling deals small, and okay them before anyone signs.
ask: What did a shark ask that you hadn't thought of?
Why did you take that deal, or walk away?
steps.tip: 'I'm out' isn't a failure. Ask that shark what would have changed their mind, and write it down.

levels.explore: Pitch to one shark and answer two questions.
levels.develop: Pitch to two or three sharks, answer every question and choose a deal.
levels.extend: Pitch twice to different sharks, change one thing in between and compare the offers.

steps.title: Make the deal real
steps.why: A handshake is easy. Paying it back is the real test.
steps.kid: Your kid writes the deal on Our deal at the end of the guide: how much, what it's for, what the shark gets back and by when. Both sign it. Then they run the business, track every payment and check in with their shark on the dates they agreed.
steps.you: Hold them to it, kindly. If they're going to be late, help them ask for more time before the date, not after.
ask: Are you on track to pay it back?
What will you tell your shark at the check-in?
steps.tip: Put the deal on the fridge and tick off each payment. Watching what they owe shrink is very satisfying.

levels.explore: Write the deal with a grown-up, and make the first payment.
levels.develop: Sign the deal, keep a payment record and check in once.
levels.extend: Pay it all back, then write what you'd ask for differently next time.

conclusion.headline: They asked for real backing, and they kept their word.
conclusion.text: Their asks change after this. If the next request comes with a reason, an amount and a payback date, the pitch has stuck.
conclusion.celebrate: On the day they make the last payment, say: 'You said you would, and you did.'
extensions: Pitch to a shark outside the family, like an aunt or a family friend
Turn the profit into a second, bigger ask
Be the shark for a sibling or a friend, and use the Shark panel card
Write down the best question any shark asked, and why it was hard

signs: They ask with numbers, not just please
They think about what the other person gets
They keep track of what they owe
makeItReal: The next time they ask for something big, ask for the pitch instead of a yes or no.
